sections.text: ## Magna Carta and the Barons (1215)

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### What Happened

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: King John of England (reigned 1199–1216) was a uniquely bad king in specific ways that matter: he lost Normandy (1204), exhausted the treasury, levied arbitrary taxes, imprisoned barons without trial, and defied the Pope (provoking an interdict that closed all churches in England). By 1215, the barons were in open revolt. They took London. John had no choice.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: **Runnymede, June 15, 1215**: John sealed Magna Carta — 63 clauses covering everything from feudal obligations to fish weirs on the Thames.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### What the Clauses Actually Said

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Most of Magna Carta is mundane feudal administration. The historically significant clauses:

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
| Clause | Content | Long-term significance |
|--------|---------|----------------------|
| 39 | "No free man shall be seized, imprisoned... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land" | Habeas corpus; due process; foundation of rule of law |
| 40 | "To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice" | Independence of courts from executive |
| 12 | Extraordinary taxes require consent of the kingdom | Parliamentary control of taxation (developed much later) |
| 61 | 25-baron committee empowered to enforce the charter | First constitutional enforcement mechanism (failed immediately) |

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: **Clause 39 is the load-bearing pillar.** Everything built on the idea that the executive cannot imprison people arbitrarily traces to this clause — through Coke, Locke, the English Bill of Rights (1689), the 5th Amendment (US), and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948).

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### What Happened Immediately After

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: John appealed to the Pope, who annulled the charter as "shameful, demeaning, illegal, and unjust." John died in 1216 (dysentery). His nine-year-old son became Henry III. The regency government reissued Magna Carta — slightly revised, stripped of the enforcement clause — to win baronial loyalty during a succession crisis. It became standard practice to reissue it.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

```
  MAGNA CARTA'S LIFECYCLE:
  ========================

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

1600s: Sir Edward Coke reinterprets it as fundamental law
         constraining both king AND parliament
         → "Magna Carta will have no sovereign" (Coke)
         → American colonists deploy this argument against Parliament
```

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### The "Great Charter" Myth

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Magna Carta as a document protecting individual rights against tyranny is largely a 17th-century invention. In 1215, it was a feudal settlement protecting barons' property rights against royal expropriation. The document says "free men" (*liberi homines*) — in 1215, perhaps 10% of the English population; serfs had no protection under it.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: What makes it historically important: (1) the principle that the king is *under* the law, not above it — which was genuinely novel as enforceable doctrine; (2) Edward Coke's early-17th-century reinterpretation, which read it as protecting all English subjects; and (3) the American colonists' deployment of that reinterpretation as a weapon against Parliament.

sections.text: ## Simon de Montfort and Parliament (1265)

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Context

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Henry III (1216–1272) governed badly, spent money lavishly on foreign wars and relatives, and repeatedly violated the principles barons thought Magna Carta established. Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, led the baronial reform movement. After his military victory over Henry at the Battle of Lewes (1264), de Montfort controlled the kingdom for 14 months.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### The Parliament of January 1265

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
De Montfort summoned a parliament that included, for the first time:
- Two knights from each county
- Two burgesses from each town

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: This was the innovation. Previous councils had been baronial assemblies. De Montfort included the *commons* — knights and townspeople — in part to build a broader coalition for his regime, in part because he apparently believed representation should extend beyond the nobility.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
```
  DE MONTFORT'S PARLIAMENT vs. EARLIER COUNCILS
  ===============================================

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
EARLIER:                      DE MONTFORT'S (1265):
  +------------------+          +------------------+
  | King             |          | King             |
  | Great lords      |          | Great lords      |
  | Bishops          |          | Bishops          |
  | (Invited who     |          | 2 knights/county |
  |  king wanted)    |          | 2 burgesses/town |
  +------------------+          +------------------+
                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                 THESE ARE NEW
                                 Commons = representative assembly
```

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### De Montfort's Death (1265)

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Henry III's son, the future Edward I, defeated de Montfort at the Battle of Evesham. De Montfort was killed; his body was mutilated. Henry III restored his prerogatives.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: But Edward I, crowned 1272, kept the parliament model. His "Model Parliament" of 1295 included representatives from counties, cities, and boroughs alongside lords and clergy — essentially the Edwardian formalization of de Montfort's improvisation.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Counterfactual

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Without de Montfort's improvisation in 1265: representative assemblies in England might have developed differently, or more slowly. The specific form — two chambers, commons separate from lords — is traceable to this moment. The American colonial assemblies and Congress are downstream of this model.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Why de Montfort Matters More Than He's Remembered

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: De Montfort is not well-known in American or world history, but his specific innovation — adding non-noble representatives to a royal council and calling it a parliament — is the institutional DNA of every legislature that includes elected representatives from geographic constituencies. Madison and Jefferson did not invent representative government; they inherited a 500-year-old English practice.

sections.text: ## Martin Luther (1483–1546)

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: On October 31, 1517, Luther nailed (or sent by letter — historians dispute) 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg. The theses attacked the sale of *indulgences* — certificates sold by the Church purporting to reduce time in purgatory. Within weeks, printed copies spread across Europe.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: This was not the first critique of Church corruption. What made it different: the printing press.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
```
  LUTHER + PRINTING PRESS AS SYSTEM
  ===================================

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
Wycliffe (1380s): Similar ideas → handwritten copies → limited spread
  Hus (1415): Similar ideas → council convened → burned at stake
  Luther (1517): 95 theses → Gutenberg press (1440) = 50 years old
                           → Thousands of copies within weeks
                           → Pope cannot control information distribution
                           → Frederick III (Elector of Saxony) protects Luther
                              (political interest in weakening papal authority)
                           → Diet of Worms (1521): Luther refuses to recant
                           → Excommunicated; translates Bible into German
                           → Vernacular scripture = individual reading =
                              priests not required as intermediaries
```

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Luther's Political Consequences

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Luther did not intend a political revolution. His intent was theological reform. The political consequences were seismic:

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
| Political Effect | Mechanism |
|-----------------|-----------|
| Princes adopted Lutheranism to seize Church properties | *Cuius regio* logic: prince's religion = territory's religion |
| Weakened papal authority over secular rulers | Undermined the Pope's ability to excommunicate and sanction kings |
| German nationalism proto-form | Luther's German Bible created a common written standard — linguistic unification predating political unification by 350 years |
| Peasants' War (1524–25) | Peasants misread Luther's spiritual freedom as social freedom; Luther repudiated them viciously |
| Fragmentation of Christendom | No single religious authority → competing denominations → eventually, tolerance as necessity |
| Thirty Years' War (1618–48) | Protestant vs. Catholic conflict → 8 million dead → Peace of Westphalia |

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Luther and Tolerance

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Luther is *not* a figure of religious tolerance. He was virulently anti-Semitic (his 1543 tract "On the Jews and Their Lies" called for burning synagogues and expelling Jews; it was cited by Nazi propagandists). He supported brutal suppression of the Peasants' War. His contribution was fracturing religious authority, not advocating pluralism.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Legacy

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: The Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War, established the principle of state sovereignty — that rulers govern within their borders free from external religious authority. This is the foundation of modern international law. It is downstream of the Reformation, which is downstream of Luther. The path runs: Luther's challenge to papal authority → religious fragmentation → wars of religion → sovereignty doctrine as the only stable settlement → Westphalian international order → UN Charter (1945).

sections.text: ## John Calvin (1509–1564)

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Calvin arrived in Geneva in 1536, was expelled, returned in 1541, and governed it as a theocratic republic until his death. His contribution is less institutional reform than intellectual architecture.

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: **Calvinist theological innovations with political consequences:**

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
| Doctrine | Political implication |
|----------|----------------------|
| Predestination | "Elect" status unknowable → visible success = possible sign of grace → Protestant work ethic (Weber's thesis) |
| Covenant theology | Government rests on covenant between ruler, people, and God → if ruler violates covenant, resistance justified |
| Consistory model | Church independent of state, with its own authority → church-state tension as constitutional framework |
| Vocation (calling) | Every occupation has religious dignity → no sacred/secular hierarchy → bourgeois culture |

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: ### Calvin's Influence on Politics

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Calvinist covenant theology directly influenced the theoretical justification for resistance to tyranny:

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
```
  CALVINIST POLITICAL THEOLOGY → CONSTITUTIONAL THEORY
  ======================================================

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
Calvinist resistance theory (Huguenots, Scots):
  → If ruler violates covenant, resistance is justified
  → Vindiciae contra Tyrannos (1579): anonymous Huguenot tract
    "Against tyrants" — systematic theory of resistance

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
John Knox (Scotland): → Presbyterian church government
                           (elders elected, not appointed)
                           → democratic structure within church
                           → model for civil representation

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
Puritans (England, then New England):
  → Calvinist covenant theology
  → Mayflower Compact (1620): covenant = founding document
  → Town meeting = congregational church meeting applied to
     civic governance
  → John Winthrop's "city on a hill" = theocratic ideal that
     secularizes into American exceptionalism
```

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text: Max Weber's thesis (*The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism*, 1905) that Calvinist predestination created the psychological preconditions for capitalist accumulation remains contested but influential. The mechanism: if success signals election, then worldly success becomes a spiritual obligation, and accumulation (rather than spending) becomes a virtue.

sections.text: ## Comparison Table

metadata.title: Medieval and Early Modern Reformers: Magna Carta, de Montfort, Luther, Calvin

sections.text:
| Figure | Period | Core Contribution | Method | Durability |
|--------|--------|------------------|--------|------------|
| Magna Carta barons | 1215 | Rule of law; executive under law | Armed confrontation + negotiation | Charter survives; specific provisions revised but principle endures |
| Simon de Montfort | 1265 | Commons in parliament; representative assembly | Military victory + governance experiment | Model Parliament (1295) formalizes it; lasts to present |
| Martin Luther | 1517–1546 | Fractured religious monopoly; vernacular scripture | Publishing + political protection | Permanent religious fragmentation; Westphalian sovereignty |
| John Calvin | 1536–1564 | Covenant theology; theocratic governance model | Institutional control of Geneva | Calvinist political theory → Puritan revolution → American constitutionalism |
